evals.prompt:
# Export failures only show up after the request is over

## Problem Description

`src/exportQueue.js` runs dataset exports. `submitExport` does a cheap check
of the request and hands back an accepted response with a job id; the work
happens later, when a worker calls `runNext`. Almost everything that can go
wrong is invisible at submit time - the dataset may have been deleted, the
requester's grant may have been revoked since they clicked the button, the row
count may be over the ceiling, object storage may be down.

Permanent failures end the job where they are found. A storage outage is
treated as worth retrying, up to a ceiling, and only then becomes a terminal
failure.

Users report "my export just never appeared", and we cannot tell them why,
because nothing in the suite covers a job that fails. The one test we have
submits an export and watches it produce a file.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/exportQueue.test.js` covering the failure paths, both the ones the
   submit step can see and the ones only the worker can.
2. Every failed job must be pinned to its own terminal record - a change that
   swapped one failure reason for another, produced a file anyway, or retried
   a permanent failure must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/exportQueue.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/exportQueue.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/exportQueue.test.js` covering the failure paths, both the ones the
   submit step can see and the ones only the worker can.
2. Every failed job must be pinned to its own terminal record - a change that
   swapped one failure reason for another, produced a file anyway, or retried
   a permanent failure must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/exportQueue.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/exportQueue.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
assertions: A file src/exportQueue.test.js exists and contains at least one failure case. A file that only repeats the successful export scores zero.

For a missing dataset, a revoked grant and an oversized dataset, the suite drives the worker and asserts the stored job has state 'failed' with the exact errorCode - DATASET_MISSING, PERMISSION_REVOKED, DATASET_TOO_LARGE. Expecting submitExport to refuse these, or asserting a throw from it, scores zero: the submit step cannot see any of them. Covering fewer than two of the three scores at most half.

At least one case asserts that a request destined to fail is still accepted at submit time - status 202 with a jobId - before the worker runs. Omitting this scores zero: it is the distinction between a refusal and a late failure.
Failure cases assert queue.artifacts stays empty. A suite that never inspects the artifact list scores zero - it passes against a worker that wrote the file and then marked the job failed.
A permanent-failure case asserts attempts is exactly 1 and queue.pending is empty afterwards. Asserting the failure state without the attempt count scores at most half; asserting neither scores zero.

A storage-outage case asserts the job returns to state 'queued' after the first run rather than failing, and that after the queue is drained it is 'failed' with STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE at exactly MAX_ATTEMPTS attempts. Treating the outage as an immediate failure scores zero; asserting the final state without the intermediate requeue or without the attempt count scores at most half.

Cases cover DATASET_REQUIRED, FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED and REQUESTER_REQUIRED with status 400 and jobId null, and assert queue.jobs is still empty and queue.seq did not advance. Asserting only the status scores at most half; omitting these cases scores zero.

No case asserts merely that the job is not 'succeeded', that errorCode is truthy, or that the artifact count is not 1. Every failure names the exact state and errorCode. Any case relying on a not-equal or truthiness check for the failure itself scores zero on this criterion - a job stuck in 'running' would satisfy it.

# Create-project handler has only a happy-path test

## Problem Description

`src/createProject.js` is the request handler behind `POST /projects`. It
validates the payload and returns a status plus a structured body.

The only test asserts a valid payload returns 201. Every rejection path the
handler implements is untested, and last month a validator regression turned
a 400 into a 500 without any test noticing.

## Output Specification

Add `src/createProject.test.js` covering the rejection paths this handler
implements, so that a rejection returning the wrong status or the wrong error
shape fails the suite.

Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.

Leave `src/createProject.happy.test.js` in place.
evals.expected_output:
Add `src/createProject.test.js` covering the rejection paths this handler
implements, so that a rejection returning the wrong status or the wrong error
shape fails the suite.

Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.

Leave `src/createProject.happy.test.js` in place.
assertions: A file src/createProject.test.js exists and contains at least one test.

Each rejection case asserts a specific numeric status - 400 for validation, 401 for authentication. Any case asserting only that the status is not 201, or only that it is 'an error', scores zero on this criterion: such a test passes on a 500 and cannot catch the regression described in the task.

Cases assert the specific error key and code - for example body.errors.name equal to TOO_LONG - rather than the presence of an errors object or a substring match on prose. Asserting only that `errors` exists, or matching on message text, scores zero here.

A missing authorization header and a present-but-wrong token are covered as separate cases asserting MISSING_TOKEN and INVALID_TOKEN respectively. Covering only one caps this at half.
A case supplies an unsupported visibility value and asserts UNSUPPORTED.

MUST NOT collapse the rejection paths into one test containing many assertions. Cases are separate tests or generated per-case, so a single failure identifies which category broke. A single mega-test scores zero here.

evals.prompt:
# Search endpoint has no coverage for hostile input

## Problem Description

`src/searchNotes.js` backs the note search box. A search term is user input
that reaches two dangerous places: the database statement and the rendered
HTML of the results page.

The handler is deliberate about both. The term itself is never part of the
statement text - it travels as a bound parameter, so a term full of quotes and
comment markers is a perfectly ordinary search that simply finds nothing. The
sort direction is different: it is interpolated into the statement, so it is
taken from a fixed map and anything else is refused. Everything the handler
renders is escaped on the way out.

A pen-test report came back with a list of strings the tester submitted -
injection attempts and markup payloads. None of them broke anything, and none
of them are in the suite either. The one test we have searches for the word
"backup".

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/searchNotes.test.js` covering how this handler treats hostile
   input, including the injection and markup strings an attacker would
   actually send.
2. A change that put a search term into the statement text, or that returned
   an unescaped term or title, must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/searchNotes.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/searchNotes.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/searchNotes.test.js` covering how this handler treats hostile
   input, including the injection and markup strings an attacker would
   actually send.
2. A change that put a search term into the statement text, or that returned
   an unescaped term or title, must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/searchNotes.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/searchNotes.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
assertions: A file src/searchNotes.test.js exists and contains at least one case built from a hostile input. A file that only repeats the word search scores zero.

For each injection payload the suite asserts status 200, that query.sql does not contain the payload or its comment marker, and that query.params[0] contains the payload verbatim. Expecting a 4xx for these payloads scores zero - it contradicts the handler and would drive the parameter binding out. Asserting only the status, or only that no exception was raised, also scores zero.

Markup payloads assert the escaped form in the rendered fields: echoHtml contains no raw angle brackets, and a matching row's titleHtml contains the entity-escaped script tag rather than the literal one. Asserting only the status for markup payloads scores zero; checking echoHtml but never a rendered result row scores at most half.

Cases send sort values outside the fixed map - including one shaped like an appended clause and one inherited object key such as toString or constructor - and assert 400 with SORT_UNSUPPORTED, plus one case asserting an allowed sort reaches the statement. Leaving sort untested scores zero: it is the only position the term-binding argument does not protect.

At least two distinct injection strings and two distinct markup strings are used, driven from a table or list rather than hand-written one at a time. One payload per class scores at most half; a single payload overall scores zero.

A term of exactly MAX_QUERY_LENGTH characters asserts 200, one character longer asserts 400 with QUERY_TOO_LONG, and a term containing a control character such as a NUL asserts 400 with QUERY_ILLEGAL_CHARACTERS. Covering none of these scores zero; testing the over-length case without the accepted boundary scores at most half.
A non-string term asserts QUERY_REQUIRED and a whitespace-only term asserts QUERY_EMPTY, each with status 400. Covering neither scores zero.

No hostile-input case has as its only assertion that the call did not throw, that a result object came back, or that the status was 200. Every such case asserts either the exact refusal or the specific safe treatment - bound parameter, escaped output. Any case whose assertions would hold with the payload concatenated into the statement scores zero on this criterion.

evals.prompt:
# Retried captures charged some customers twice

## Problem Description

`src/capturePayment.js` is the capture step behind `POST /payments/capture`.
Our mobile client retries any request whose response it never saw, so the same
capture arrives two or three times with the same `Idempotency-Key`.

In March that produced 41 double charges. The handler now records the key with
a fingerprint of the request and replays the stored outcome instead of moving
money again. Support also hit the other side of it: a customer whose first
attempt was refused for a bad amount could not retry under the same key,
because the old code recorded the key before validating.

The suite has one test - a first capture succeeds. Nothing exercises a retry,
so the replay bookkeeping could be deleted without turning the build red.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/capturePayment.test.js` covering the retry and rejection paths.
2. A change that charged twice for a replay, or that made a refused key
   unusable, must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/capturePayment.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/capturePayment.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/capturePayment.test.js` covering the retry and rejection paths.
2. A change that charged twice for a replay, or that made a refused key
   unusable, must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/capturePayment.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/capturePayment.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
assertions: A file src/capturePayment.test.js exists and contains at least one test beyond a repeat of the success path. A file with no retry or rejection case scores zero.

The identical-retry case asserts gateway.charges.length is still 1 after the second call, so a handler that charged twice and echoed the first id fails. A suite that asserts only the status, code or chargeId of the replay scores zero on this criterion - none of those detect a second charge.

The identical retry asserts status 200, replayed true, and the same chargeId the first call returned. Asserting 201 or a 4xx for an identical retry scores zero: it contradicts the handler and would drive the replay behaviour back out.

A case sends a request that fails validation under a fresh key, then re-sends a valid body under that same key and asserts status 201 with replayed false and exactly one charge. Omitting this case scores zero; asserting the first refusal without the successful retry under the same key scores at most half.

A case reuses a key with a changed amount or customer and asserts status 409 with IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED, chargeId null, and gateway.charges.length still 1. Asserting the 409 without the charge count scores at most half; asserting neither scores zero.

Malformed input asserts 400 with its exact code (IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED, CUSTOMER_REQUIRED, AMOUNT_NOT_AN_INTEGER, CURRENCY_UNSUPPORTED) while a well-formed but unacceptable amount asserts 422 with AMOUNT_NOT_POSITIVE or AMOUNT_ABOVE_LIMIT. A suite expecting 400 for the amount cases, or expecting the same status across both families, scores zero.
At least one refusal case asserts gateway.charges.length is 0 and gateway.keys.size is 0 after the call. Never inspecting the gateway on a refusal scores zero.

amountCents is covered both as a string such as '2500' - the shape the retrying mobile client sends - and as a non-integer number such as 25.5, each asserting AMOUNT_NOT_AN_INTEGER. Omitting type mismatches entirely scores zero; covering only one of the two scores at most half.

# Bulk member import: a rejected batch used to leave half the rows behind

## Problem Description

`src/importMembers.js` is the handler behind `POST /directories/:id/members:import`.
It takes a batch of rows and either applies all of them or applies none.

Two releases ago it applied rows as it walked the batch, so a bad row at
position 9 left rows 0 to 8 in the directory and 9 lines in the audit log. An
admin then re-sent the corrected batch and got a duplicate-email refusal for
rows that were never supposed to exist. The handler was rewritten to stage the
batch first; the current file is that rewrite.

The only test is the success case. Nothing in the suite would notice if the
staging step were dropped again - the refusal status would still be the same,
and that is all anyone checks today.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/importMembers.test.js` covering the refusal paths this handler
   implements.
2. A refusal that returned the right status while still writing rows, audit
   lines, or id sequence numbers must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/importMembers.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/importMembers.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/importMembers.test.js` covering the refusal paths this handler
   implements.
2. A refusal that returned the right status while still writing rows, audit
   lines, or id sequence numbers must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/importMembers.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/importMembers.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
assertions: A file src/importMembers.test.js exists and contains at least one test that exercises a refusal. A file that only re-tests the success path scores zero.

Refusal cases assert the observable side effects did not happen: directory.members.size, directory.audit.length and directory.seq all hold their pre-call values. A suite where no case inspects the directory after a refusal scores zero - it cannot distinguish a staged batch from a half-applied one. Inspecting the directory in only one case scores at most half.

At least one case sends a batch of three or more rows whose first valid rows precede an invalid one (index 1 or later), asserts the returned index identifies that row, and asserts nothing was written. A suite whose invalid rows are all at index 0 scores zero here: no earlier row existed to leak.

Each case pins a specific numeric status and the exact code string the handler returns - 400 with ROW_MALFORMED / EMAIL_INVALID / ROLE_UNSUPPORTED, 409 with EMAIL_DUPLICATE, 422 with BATCH_TOO_LARGE. Any case that asserts only that the status is not 201, or only that imported is not 2, scores zero.

A case imports a member, then re-imports the same email with a different role, and asserts the stored record still carries the original role and that no audit line was appended. Asserting only the 409 scores zero on this criterion.

One case duplicates an email inside a single batch and a separate case collides with a member already in the directory, each asserting the index of the row that collided. Covering only one of the two scores at most half; covering neither scores zero.

Cases cover a batch that is not an array, an empty batch, and a batch above MAX_BATCH, each asserting its own code and asserting index is null. Missing all three scores zero; the oversize case asserting 400 rather than 422 scores at most half.

No case asserts merely that a code is present or truthy, that status is greater than or equal to 400, or that the result is 'an error'. Every refusal names the exact code, and where the handler supplies one, the exact index. Any case relying on a truthiness or not-equal check for the refusal itself scores zero on this criterion.

# Throttling and plan limits are only covered by the success case

## Problem Description

`src/sendMessage.js` sits behind `POST /messages`. Two separate limits apply
to it: a short burst limit per API key inside a rolling window, and a monthly
allowance per account tied to the plan. They are different refusals - one
clears on its own, the other does not until the customer upgrades - and
support answers them with different replies.

The clock is passed in as `now`, so the whole thing is drivable from a test
without waiting or faking timers.

Last quarter a change to the window bookkeeping made a throttled call consume
the caller's monthly allowance. Customers on the free plan burned their month
in an afternoon of retries. The only test we have sends one message and checks
it was delivered.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/sendMessage.test.js` covering the refusal paths, driving `now`
   explicitly rather than waiting on real time.
2. A refused call that still delivered a message or still consumed monthly
   allowance must fail the suite, and the two refusal families must not be
   interchangeable.
3. Do not modify `src/sendMessage.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/sendMessage.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/sendMessage.test.js` covering the refusal paths, driving `now`
   explicitly rather than waiting on real time.
2. A refused call that still delivered a message or still consumed monthly
   allowance must fail the suite, and the two refusal families must not be
   interchangeable.
3. Do not modify `src/sendMessage.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/sendMessage.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
assertions: A file src/sendMessage.test.js exists and contains at least one refusal case. A file that only repeats the delivery path scores zero.

Within one window the suite asserts the fifth call still returns 202 and the sixth returns 429, rather than looping until some call is refused. A suite that never asserts the status of the last accepted call, or that discovers the refusal with an unbounded loop or a while condition, scores zero: an off-by-one in BURST_LIMIT passes it unchanged.

The throttled case asserts the precise retryAfterMs the handler computes from the window start and the supplied now - for example 59970 for a window opened at 1000 and a call at 1030. Asserting only that retryAfterMs is present, truthy, or greater than zero scores zero.

After a 429 the suite asserts state.delivered length and the account's entry in state.usage are unchanged from before the refused call. Never inspecting state after a refusal scores zero - this is the regression the task describes.

A case advances now by at least WINDOW_MS after a refusal and asserts a full burst is accepted again, showing the throttle is temporary. Omitting it scores zero; asserting only one accepted call after the advance rather than the restored burst scores at most half.

A case drives the free account to its monthly allowance across successive windows and asserts status 403 with QUOTA_EXHAUSTED and retryAfterMs null, plus a later call in a still-later window that is refused the same way. Expecting 429 for the allowance case, or asserting the same status for both limits, scores zero; omitting the proof that it does not clear with the next window scores at most half.
An unknown API key asserts 401 with API_KEY_UNKNOWN and an empty or non-string body asserts 400 with BODY_REQUIRED, each also asserting nothing was delivered. Covering neither scores zero.

No case asserts merely that the status is not 202, is at least 400, or that a code is set. Every refusal names its exact status and code, so a 500 in place of a 429 fails. Any case relying on a not-equal or truthiness check for the refusal scores zero on this criterion.

## Problem Description

`src/updateSettings.js` applies a partial settings update. Each field has a
declared type, and the handler rejects anything that does not match.

We shipped a bug where `itemsPerPage` arrived as the string `"25"` from an
older mobile client and was stored as a string, which broke pagination
downstream. The handler does reject it now, but nothing tests that it does -
and the same hole exists for the other fields.

## Output Specification

Add `src/updateSettings.test.js` covering the wrong-type rejection for every
field this handler accepts, plus the value-level rejections it implements.

Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.

Leave `src/updateSettings.happy.test.js` in place.

Add `src/updateSettings.test.js` covering the wrong-type rejection for every
field this handler accepts, plus the value-level rejections it implements.

Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.

Leave `src/updateSettings.happy.test.js` in place.
assertions: A file src/updateSettings.test.js exists and contains at least one test.

All four fields - theme, notificationsEnabled, itemsPerPage, tags - each have a case supplying a value of the wrong type and asserting WRONG_TYPE on that field. Score proportionally: four fields covered is full marks, three is three quarters, two is half, one or none scores zero.

evals.prompt:
# Order status changes: every refusal looks the same from the outside

## Problem Description

`src/orderState.js` moves an order between statuses. Callers must send the
version they read, so two operators editing the same order at once cannot
silently overwrite each other.

The refusals are not one thing. A caller who sent no version at all is missing
a precondition. A caller whose version is behind read a stale copy and should
re-read and retry. A caller asking for a move the workflow does not allow has
a bug and retrying will never help. A caller asking for the status the order is
already in, and a caller trying to move an order that has reached the end of
its life, are two more cases again - the support macros for those two differ,
and both come back with the same numeric status, so the code is the only thing
that tells them apart.

Only the success path is tested. Last sprint a refactor made a stale version
report as an illegal move, and the client retried forever.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/orderState.test.js` covering the refusal paths, keeping every
   refusal reason distinguishable from the others.
2. A refusal that advanced the order's version or appended an event must fail
   the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/orderState.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/orderState.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/orderState.test.js` covering the refusal paths, keeping every
   refusal reason distinguishable from the others.
2. A refusal that advanced the order's version or appended an event must fail
   the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/orderState.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/orderState.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
assertions: A file src/orderState.test.js exists and contains at least one refusal case. A file that only repeats the successful placement scores zero.

The suite asserts 404 for an unknown order, 428 for an absent version precondition, 412 for a stale version, 422 for an unknown status and for a disallowed move, and 409 for the repeat and finalised cases. Any two families sharing an expected status where the handler distinguishes them scores zero, as does a suite expecting 400 for the validation-shaped refusals.

After each refusal the suite asserts the order's status and version are exactly what they were before the call and that store.events is still empty. A suite that never inspects the stored order after a refusal scores zero; inspecting it after only one refusal scores at most half.

A case sends a stale version together with a move that is also disallowed and asserts VERSION_STALE, showing the precondition is evaluated first, and a case sends an unknown order id together with an invalid status and asserts ORDER_NOT_FOUND. Neither case present scores zero; one of the two scores at most half.

On the finalised order, asking for the status it already holds asserts ALREADY_IN_STATUS while asking for another status asserts ORDER_FINALISED, both with status 409 and both asserted on the code. Asserting only the numeric status for these scores zero: 409 alone cannot tell the two support responses apart.
At least one refusal case asserts currentVersion carries the order's actual current version, which is what lets a client re-read and retry. Never asserting it scores zero.

A case omits ifMatch entirely - and a second passes null - asserting 428 with IF_MATCH_REQUIRED, kept distinct from the stale-version case. Folding the missing precondition into the stale case scores zero.

The refusal families are separate test functions, or generated per case from a table with individually named cases, so a single failure identifies which family broke. One test containing every refusal assertion in sequence scores zero: the first failing assertion masks every family after it.

# Webhook endpoint answers every bad request the same way in our tests

## Problem Description

`src/receiveWebhook.js` is the entry point for partner webhooks. It works on
the raw request - headers plus the unparsed body string - because the
signature covers the exact bytes we received.

The checks run in a fixed order for a reason. We refuse a body we are not
willing to read before we read it, and we verify the signature before handing
anything to the parser, so a hostile sender cannot reach `JSON.parse` at all.
Partners integrate against the specific statuses: their retry logic backs off
on some and gives up on others.

Support spent a week on a partner whose payloads were rejected while their
staging traffic worked. The cause was a body under our character limit but
over our byte limit once accented characters were counted. Our suite has one
test - a correctly signed ping is accepted.

## Output Specification

1. Add `src/receiveWebhook.test.js` covering the rejection paths, including
   the order in which the checks apply.
2. A change that answered a rejected request with a different status, or that
   parsed a body it should have refused first, must fail the suite.
3. Do not modify `src/receiveWebhook.js`; its current behaviour is the
   specification.
4. Leave `src/receiveWebhook.happy.test.js` in place.
5. Run `npm test` before you finish; it must pass.
evals.expected_output:
1. Add `src/receiveWebhook.test.js` covering the rejection paths, including
